slides.title: One Solution, No Solution, Infinitely Many Solutions
slides.note: Post the learning target. Today is 43 minutes: the cut is under Materials at the end of this edition.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Q4 is today's question in miniature: a solution is a number that makes the equation true. Today some equations have no such number and some have every number. Two minutes silent, then reveal, no discussion — 43 minutes today: the cut is under Materials.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Vocabulary
slides.sub: The new words, before they are used.
slides.note: Two names for the two new endings. Under each, say the ending aloud: 5 = 9 is never true, whatever x was — no number works; 5 = 5 is always true, whatever x was — every number works. 'One solution' needs no definition: it is every equation of the last two days.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Three equations that differ by one number. Take 2x from both sides of each. The first leaves 5 = x + 9, so x = −4: one solution. The second leaves 5 = 9 — no x left, and 5 = 9 is never true, whatever x was: no solution. The third leaves 5 = 5 — always true, whatever x was: every number works, infinitely many solutions. The ending is a sentence about numbers; read it for what it says. We know 5 = 9 is never true without trying a single number — the x's are gone, so no number can change it.
OFF: 'x = a: one. A false sentence: none. A true sentence: every number.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Simplify each side first — distribute, collect — THEN compare. 3(x + 2) is 3x + 6, so the first equation has the same thing on both sides: infinitely many. In the second, the x-terms are the same (3x) and the constants differ (6 and 2): taking 3x leaves 6 = 2, never true. Different x-terms always leave an x, so one solution. The comparison is made only after simplifying: 2x + 5 − 1 = 2x + 4 looks like different constants until the left side is collected (audit T6).
OFF: 'Same x-terms, same constants: every number. Same x-terms, different constants: none. Different x-terms: one.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Add 2x to both sides: 6x + 7 = 7. Subtract 7: 6x = 0, so x = 0. An x is still there, so this is x = a — one solution, and the solution is 0. 'No solution' is wrong: 0 works. Check: 4(0) + 7 = 7 and 7 − 2(0) = 7. The B1G-M names this one: a student who expects 'x = a number' reads 6x = 0 as 'nothing'.
OFF: 'x = 0 is an answer. Zero is a number.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Ask what the left side is once it is simplified, before anyone takes a term away.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Distribute and collect: the left side is 4x − 10, the same as the right. Taking 4x from both sides leaves −10 = −10, true whatever x was: infinitely many solutions. A board with 'x = −10' read the constant as the answer; one with 'no solution' saw the x's vanish and stopped.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 6x + 3 − 5 = 6x − 2, the same as the right side; −2 = −2, infinitely many. This catches 'x = −2' (the constant read as the answer) and 'no solution' (the x's gone, so 'nothing'). The verdict is Example 1's, so look for the LINE on the boards — −2 = −2 (or 6x − 2 = 6x − 2) and 'always true' — not the words.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.sub: The x-terms go and the constants do not match.
slides.note: Ask what the 2 multiplies, then which x-terms are on each side once it is distributed.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Distribute: 6x + 8. The x-terms match (6x and 6x) and the constants do not (8 and 5). Taking 6x from both sides leaves 8 = 5 — a false sentence with no x left in it, so no number can make it true: no solution. Write the ending as it is, 8 = 5, with its words: never true. A board with 6x + 4 distributed to one term (and still gets no solution, by luck — say so).

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: 10x − 5 against 10x + 3: the same x-terms, different constants. Taking 10x leaves −5 = 3, never true: no solution. A board with 'x = 3' or 'x = −5' read a constant as the answer. The verdict is Example 2's, so look for the LINE — −5 = 3 and 'never true' — not the words.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: The same expression on both sides: every number works. A board with x = 2 read the constant as the answer; one with 'no solution' saw the x's go and stopped.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Same x-terms, different constants: 8 = −1 is never true. A board with 'infinitely many' saw matching x-terms and stopped (Notes II: the constants must match too); one with x = −9 or x = 9 subtracted the constants and wrote an x.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: The pattern breaks: the constants match and the x-terms do not, so an x is left — one solution, and it is 0 (Notes III). A board with 'no solution' read 3x = 0 as 'nothing'; one with 'infinitely many' saw the matching 4s. Check in both sides: 4 = 4.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. Option D reads the constant as x, option A reads 0 = 0 as x = 0, option C stops when the x's vanish. 0 and 6 do both work — and so does every other number, which is why 'one solution' is wrong. Options A and D are the same error (an ending read as x = a number) and get the same reteach: say the ending aloud, 6 = 6, and ask for which x it is true. On a split: sixty seconds, convince your neighbor, re-vote.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: An ordinary one solution, negative, behind parentheses: it looks like Example 2's kind until the 3 is distributed — 3x on the right against 6x on the left, so an x is left. Take 3x, add 9, divide by 3. A board with 'no solution' judged before distributing; one with x = 5/3 wrote 3x − 4 (one term); one with x = 7 wrote 3x + 12 (the sign); one with x = −7 subtracted the 9. Check: −15 = −15.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. Option A is today's named trap — the solution is 0, not 'none'; option C is the same expression written backwards. Ask a room that chose A to say the ending aloud: 1 = −1, never true.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: The extra-number board (ruling 22): the 8 GB limit is not needed. Both plans add \$3 a gigabyte, so B stays \$5 above A at every amount of data: 15 + 3g = 20 + 3g ends 15 = 20, never true. A board with g = 5 subtracted the monthly fees and called it gigabytes.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Backwards: choose the ending. Infinitely many needs the same thing on both sides — the right side must be 4x + 12. No solution needs the same x-term with a different constant — 6x, and −10 is already not +1. A board with 3 distributed to one term; one with 5 in the second box took the −5 from inside.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written, and the exit evidence. Read two aloud: one that names the ending (0 = 0 is always true) and one that tries a second number and sees it work — then say why trying numbers alone is not proof: the simplifying is.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Independent Set
slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in writing.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set; the same six questions are on the board. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.
